traveler: Augusta Ada King, Countess of Lovelace (Ada Byron)
title: The Loom and the Engine: Byron's Daughter, the Analytical Engine, and the Notes Signed A.A.L.
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Piccadilly Terrace, the birth
stops.date_confidence: attested; the house stood at the Hyde Park Corner end of Piccadilly Terrace, on the site now numbered 139 Piccadilly, and the pin follows that siting rather than the Green Park coordinates carried in some accounts
stops.campa: Augusta Ada Byron is born at 13 Piccadilly Terrace, the only legitimate child of the poet Lord Byron and Anne Isabella Milbanke. The marriage is already failing. The house is rented and the creditors are close. Augusta is the name of Byron's half-sister; Ada is the syllable kept back for private use. Her father sees her for the last time on 15 January 1816, at five weeks old. No object from the house is known to survive. The terrace is later renumbered into Piccadilly and the building stands on as 139.
sources: Betty Alexandra Toole, 'Ada, the Enchantress of Numbers'
suggested_refs: 139 Piccadilly, London, the renumbered site of Byron's rented house

stops.name: Kirkby Mallory, the removal
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Five weeks after the birth Annabella takes the infant out of London to her parents' house at Kirkby Mallory in Leicestershire, ostensibly for a rest cure. Byron is told the separation is temporary. Solicitors follow instead of reconciliation: her lawyers gather here the testimony that ends the marriage inside four months. Ada has no memory of arriving and will spend her childhood in the place. Kirkby Hall stands until 1952, when it is pulled down; the memorial in the village outlives the building it belonged to.
sources: Annabella Milbanke's 1816 correspondence, as printed in the standard biographies
suggested_refs: The site of Kirkby Hall, Kirkby Mallory, demolished 1952

stops.name: London, the deed of separation
stops.date_confidence: attested for the signing; the Wikipedia article on Anne Isabella Byron dates a private settlement to March 1816, and the two accounts are recorded here without being reconciled
stops.campa: Byron signs the deed of separation. The terms hand his wife the child entire. Annabella will raise her and choose her tutors, and the curriculum she sets against the father's memory is mathematics, meant to burn the poetry out of the blood. Byron never contests it and never sees the girl again. The father is absent from every room of her life and present in her name; for the next thirty-six years the rooms she enters introduce her as his daughter first.
suggested_refs: The 1816 deed of separation between Lord and Lady Byron

stops.name: Dover, the father sails
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Four days after signing, Byron takes ship at Dover and leaves England for good. Debt, scandal and the rumors about his half-sister Augusta Leigh drive him out, and he will not return alive. Ada is four months old. Her mother will spend the next years watching for the poet in the daughter. What Ada learns of her father comes from reviews and from gossip, and from the silence kept around him at home. The two dates, 21 and 25 April, are often collapsed into one.
suggested_refs: Byron's departure from Dover, 25 April 1816

stops.name: Missolonghi, the father dies
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Byron dies of fever at Missolonghi, a town held by the Greek revolution inside the Ottoman Empire, after months spent paying and drilling soldiers for a country that does not yet exist. He is thirty-six years old. Ada is eight, and has never seen him, and now never will. His body is refused Westminster Abbey and carried north to the family vault at Hucknall in Nottinghamshire. Twenty-eight years later, at the same age he reached, she asks to be laid beside him there, and is.
suggested_refs: Missolonghi in the Greek War of Independence, held ground rather than Greek territory in 1824

stops.name: Fordhook, Flyology
stops.date_confidence: the project is attested from her childhood correspondence and dated to her twelfth year; the month is conventional and no source consulted fixes the house
stops.campa: At twelve she decides she will fly. She studies the proportions of birds, weighs paper against oiled silk against feathers, designs a wing an arm could work, and plans an illustrated book on the subject; she calls the whole enterprise Flyology. Her mother, who is engineering a mathematician, does not discourage it. No manuscript of Flyology is confirmed to survive, and the episode reaches the present through letters and later retellings that give it more finish than the surviving fragments can carry.
sources: Betty Alexandra Toole, 'Ada, the Enchantress of Numbers'
suggested_refs: Ada Byron's childhood letters on Flyology, as quoted in Toole

stops.name: Fordhook, the year in bed
stops.date_confidence: attested to June 1829; the specific house is not named in the sources consulted
stops.campa: Measles takes her in June and leaves her partially paralyzed, bedridden for close to a year. Annabella nurses her on a regimen of stillness and correction, treating the paralysis as a discipline as much as a disease. Ada reads through it. By 1831 she is walking with crutches, and headaches and periods of weakness recur for the rest of her life. Some biographers credit the enforced stillness with the concentration she later brings to mathematics; the accounts that stretch the paralysis to 1832 overstate what the letters say.
sources: Annabella Milbanke's correspondence, as printed in the standard biographies
suggested_refs: The 1829-1831 illness, variously reported as measles and as a related paralytic illness

stops.name: Stamford Hill, the Frend household
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the Frend connection is traditional in the biographies and no dated visit to the Stamford Hill house is established here
stops.campa: William Frend, mathematician and radical reformer, once tutor to Annabella herself, stays inside the family circle while Ada is a child. His household is one node of a network that keeps a girl's education unusually severe: Frend, then Mary Somerville, then Augustus De Morgan, relay-tutoring across two decades. No school in England will teach a daughter what these three teach her by post and at table. Frend's own daughter Sophia becomes a family intimate in the next generation.
sources: Biographical accounts of the Frend, Milbanke and Lovelace network
suggested_refs: William Frend's Stamford Hill household, node of the tutoring network

stops.name: Hanover Square, Mary Somerville
stops.date_confidence: the friendship and the tutoring are attested; the year is conventional
stops.campa: Mary Somerville, the most celebrated woman of science in England, takes the girl seriously. She answers letters on differential calculus with a patience the hired tutors lack, and she takes the questions as questions rather than as self-improvement. Through her the girl reaches a scientific society that rank alone does not open. The friendship holds until Ada's death. Somerville outlives her by almost exactly twenty years, dying at Naples on 29 November 1872, and it is through her circle that the introduction of 1833 is made.
sources: Somerville's memoirs and the Lovelace correspondence
Siting caveat: Somerville's Hanover Square address is disputed, since her Hanover Square residence is elsewhere tied to her husband's 1819 Chelsea Hospital appointment; the pin is provisional
suggested_refs: Mary Somerville's London house and the Lovelace correspondence on calculus

stops.name: St James's Palace, presented at Court
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1833; the exact date of the presentation is not fixed here
stops.campa: At seventeen she is presented at Court, the ritual that launches an aristocratic girl into the London season. She curtseys to the machinery of rank in the same months she is shown the machinery of calculation. Annabella has spent seventeen years managing this single entrance. The season it opens is a circuit of balls, dinners and scientific evenings, and it is on that circuit, within weeks, that she is introduced to a man building a brass engine which does arithmetic without a mind behind it.
suggested_refs: The 1833 London season and the presentation at Court

stops.name: Dorset Street, the introduction to Babbage
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: At one of Charles Babbage's Saturday evenings she is introduced to him, brought into the room by her mother and Mary Somerville. Babbage is forty-one and holds the Lucasian chair at Cambridge that Isaac Newton held before him, a chain of the same professorship running from Barrow to Newton to this table. She is seventeen. The room is full of people who have come to admire a curiosity. The acquaintance made here runs nineteen years, and produces the one paper she publishes.
sources: The Lucasian chair link to Newton is inferred from outside knowledge; no file in this corpus states Babbage's tenure, and the connection is flagged as reconstruction
suggested_refs: Babbage's Saturday soirees at 1 Dorset Street, Marylebone

stops.name: Dorset Street, the portion of the Difference Engine
stops.date_confidence: the visit is attested to June 1833, a fortnight or so after the introduction; the day is conventional
stops.campa: Two weeks later she is shown the unfinished Difference Engine, a portion of brass and steel gearing built to calculate polynomial tables with no human error in them. The other guests admire the demonstration. She asks how it works, and then asks for the drawings. Babbage is said to have called her the Enchantress of Number, a phrase repeated everywhere and traced by nobody to a letter that can be produced. The house on Dorset Street becomes a fixed address in her life for nineteen years.
sources: The phrase 'Enchantress of Number' could not be traced to any primary text fetched, including the Gutenberg text of Babbage's 'Passages from the Life of a Philosopher'; treated as unverified tradition
suggested_refs: The surviving demonstration portion of Babbage's Difference Engine No. 1

stops.name: Fordhook, the tutor and the elopement
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; reported in modern biography, sourced to Betty Alexandra Toole, with limited contemporaneous documentation and no house named
stops.campa: As a teenager she has an affair with one of her tutors and attempts to elope with him. The family finds them, brings her back, and closes the matter so completely that the man's name does not survive in the record. Annabella's project of a mathematical daughter is in part a project against exactly this, the Byron temperament breaking surface. The episode reaches the present through biography rather than through documents, and stands here as tradition rather than as an attested day.
sources: Wikipedia, 'Ada Lovelace', citing Betty Alexandra Toole
suggested_refs: The 1833 elopement episode as related in Toole's biography

stops.name: The Midland mills, cards of perforated pasteboard
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the tour is standard in the biographies, but no source consulted fixes the town, the mill or the date, and the pin stands for the Nottingham and Derby mill country generally
stops.campa: Travelling through the Midlands she tours working textile mills, where power looms run under the control of punched cards. Joseph-Marie Jacquard's attachment reads a chain of holes and drives the harness accordingly: the pattern lives outside the weaver, in pasteboard, and repeats without memory and without fatigue. Nine years later she writes the sentence that will outlast every other line she leaves behind, that the Analytical Engine weaves algebraical patterns as the Jacquard loom weaves flowers and leaves, and she means the comparison as engineering, not as metaphor, a machine reading its own pattern the way the loom reads its cards.
sources: Traditional account in the Lovelace biographies; exact mill unconfirmed
suggested_refs: The Analytical Engine and the Jacquard loom, the comparison Lovelace draws in her own 1843 notes

stops.name: Fordhook, the marriage
stops.date_confidence: the date is attested; Fordhook as the venue is the standard account and is not named in every source
stops.campa: She marries William, 8th Baron King, at Fordhook: a quiet ceremony at a family house rather than a fashionable church. She is nineteen. He is steady, interested in agriculture and architecture and not at all in verse, which is the whole of Annabella's approval of him. The match brings a title, an income and three houses: Ockham Park, Ashley Combe, Horsley Towers. Within three years he is created Earl of Lovelace, and she becomes the Countess whose name the next two centuries will use.
suggested_refs: The marriage settlement of Ada Byron and William, 8th Baron King, July 1835

stops.name: Ashley Combe, the fairy palace
stops.date_confidence: the honeymoon and the annual summers are attested; the month is conventional
stops.campa: The honeymoon is spent above Porlock Weir at Ashley Combe, a hunting lodge of 1799 that King remodels and extends for twenty years into terraces and towers cut into a wooded Somerset combe over the Bristol Channel. She calls it her fairy palace and returns every summer of her life. Much of the 1843 correspondence with Babbage passes through this post: the arithmetic of London worked out in a house chosen for sea air and silence. King is still building when she dies.
sources: Betty Alexandra Toole, 'Ada, the Enchantress of Numbers'
suggested_refs: The terraces and tunnels of Ashley Combe above Porlock Weir, Somerset

stops.name: Ockham Park, the three children
stops.date_confidence: the births of 1836, 1837 and 1839 are attested; the pin is the family seat rather than a named room, and the 1837 illness is reported in two irreconcilable versions
stops.campa: At Ockham Park, built about 1638 and in the King family since the 1720s, she bears three children in four years: Byron in 1836, Anne Isabella in 1837, Ralph Gordon in 1839. After the second birth she is ill for months, described by those around her as tedious and suffering. One biographical account instead reports cholera in 1837, leaving asthma and digestive trouble later treated with laudanum and opium; the two versions are set down here without being reconciled. In 1838 King is created Earl of Lovelace.
suggested_refs: Ockham Park, Surrey, altered by Nicholas Hawksmoor 1727-1729

stops.name: University College London, De Morgan by post
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1840-1841
stops.campa: From 1840 she studies advanced mathematics with Augustus De Morgan, professor at University College London, almost entirely by post, since a married countess does not sit among undergraduates. He sends problem sets in calculus and algebra; she returns worked solutions, sometimes with extensions of her own. He writes to her mother that her skill might lead her to become an original mathematical investigator, perhaps of first-rate eminence. The lessons give her the technical footing the Notes will need two years later.
stops.quote: might lead her to become an original mathematical investigator, perhaps of first-rate eminence
stops.quote_source: Augustus De Morgan to Lady Byron, quoted in Wikipedia, 'Ada Lovelace'; the widely repeated gloss 'comparable to any man's' does not appear in the source and is not used here
sources: De Morgan and Annabella correspondence, quoted in the biographies
suggested_refs: The De Morgan and Lovelace correspondence on calculus, 1840-1841

stops.name: Turin, Babbage before Menabrea
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1840; the day is not fixed here
stops.campa: Babbage travels to Turin and gives a seminar on the Analytical Engine, a machine that exists as drawings and as argument and will not be built in his lifetime. Among the listeners is Luigi Federico Menabrea, a young military engineer who will end as prime minister of Italy. Menabrea takes notes and writes them up in French. The one paper Ada Lovelace publishes begins here, with an Englishman describing an unbuilt engine to an Italian room and an Italian putting it into a third language.
suggested_refs: Babbage's 1840 Turin seminar on the Analytical Engine

stops.name: Ockham Park, the letter about Medora Leigh
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the letter is dated in the biographical tradition, and its reading rests on that tradition rather than on a full published text
stops.campa: Her mother tells her at last what London has whispered since 1816: that Byron fathered a child, Medora Leigh, on his half-sister Augusta. Ada writes back accepting the revelation, and is reported unsurprised by it. The scandal that drove her father out of England before she could hold her head up is now a fact in her own hand. She is twenty-five, a countess, and three children in. The work that will carry her own initials is eighteen months away.
suggested_refs: The 27 February 1841 letter to Lady Byron on Medora Leigh

stops.name: Geneva, Menabrea in French
stops.date_confidence: attested to October 1842
stops.campa: Menabrea's account of the Turin lecture is published in Geneva as Notions sur la machine analytique de M. Charles Babbage, in the Bibliotheque universelle. It is the only substantial published description of the Analytical Engine in existence: written in French, by an Italian, about an English machine that has never been built. Babbage puts it into the hands of the one person in London he thinks capable of carrying it into English without flattening it into a description of a calculator.
suggested_refs: L. F. Menabrea, 'Notions sur la machine analytique de M. Charles Babbage' (1842)

stops.name: Dorset Street, nine months of translation
stops.date_confidence: the work spans roughly nine months across 1842 and 1843; the starting month is conventional
stops.campa: She translates Menabrea across roughly nine months. Babbage asks why she has not written an original paper on a subject she knows so well; she answers that it had not occurred to her, and then, at his urging, appends her own Notes, lettered A through G. The Notes run about three times the length of the article they are attached to. The translation is a service. The Notes are a treatise, and inside them the machine stops being a calculator and becomes a general engine for operating on symbols.
stops.quote: The Analytical Engine is an embodying of the science of operations, constructed with peculiar reference to abstract number as the subject of those operations.
stops.quote_source: Ada Lovelace, Note A to L. F. Menabrea, 'Sketch of the Analytical Engine Invented by Charles Babbage', Scientific Memoirs vol. 3 (1843)
suggested_refs: The manuscript drafts of the Notes, Lovelace papers

stops.name: Ashley Combe, the Notes by post
stops.date_confidence: the summer correspondence is attested; the month is approximate
stops.campa: Through the summer the argument travels between Somerset and Marylebone in the post: proofs, corrections, tables of operations, and a rising temper on both sides. Babbage alters her text without asking and wants an unsigned preface of his own folded into the work. She refuses. She will not have her paper carry an anonymous quarrel with the government inside it, and she keeps the Notes, and the responsibility for them, in her own hands. The tables of operations are checked line by line in a house above Porlock Weir.
suggested_refs: The 1843 Lovelace and Babbage letters over the preface and the signature

stops.name: London, the loom and the engine
stops.date_confidence: the publication year of the note is attested; the pin is inherited unchanged from the atlas, placed with the woven Jacquard portrait rather than at any address of Lovelace's
stops.campa: In Note A she sets the two machines side by side, and the sentence outlives everything else she writes. Babbage keeps a woven silk portrait of Joseph-Marie Jacquard framed in his house and shows it to Prince Albert; two Royal Academicians take the cloth for an engraving. The image is not decoration. Both machines are a chain of holes telling a mechanism what to do next, and the pattern is held outside the hand that would otherwise have to remember it.
stops.quote: We may say most aptly, that the Analytical Engine weaves algebraical patterns just as the Jacquard-loom weaves flowers and leaves.
stops.quote_source: Ada Lovelace, Note A to L. F. Menabrea, 'Sketch of the Analytical Engine Invented by Charles Babbage, Esq.', Scientific Memoirs vol. 3 (1843)
sources: Ada Lovelace, Note A to Menabrea's Sketch (1843)
Charles Babbage, 'Passages from the Life of a Philosopher', ch. VIII
joseph_marie_jacquard.journey.json, stops 'London, algebraical patterns' and 'London, the sheet mistaken for an engraving'
suggested_refs: The 1839 woven silk portrait of Jacquard, framed in Babbage's house

stops.name: London, Scientific Memoirs, signed A.A.L.
stops.date_confidence: attested to September 1843
stops.campa: The translation and the Notes appear in Richard Taylor's Scientific Memoirs, volume three, signed with three initials: A.A.L. A countess does not put her name to a scientific paper, and the initials are a concealment and a claim at once, since everyone in the room already knows whose they are. Six copies of the first-edition printing are known to survive: three at Harvard, one at the University of Oklahoma, one at the United States Air Force Academy, and one in private hands.
sources: Bonhams catalogue and bibliographic census as reported at the 2018 sale
suggested_refs: Taylor's Scientific Memoirs, vol. 3 (1843), the first-edition printing

stops.name: London, Note G and the Bernoulli numbers
stops.date_confidence: the Note is dated by its publication; the label 'first computer program' is a later historiographic claim and is not a phrase used in 1843
stops.campa: Note G sets out, step by step and with a table of operations, a method by which the Analytical Engine would compute the Bernoulli numbers. Nothing exists that could run it. Historians have argued the credit ever since: Allan Bromley holds that Babbage had prepared such programs years earlier, Stephen Wolfram that her exposition is cleaner and more sophisticated than Babbage's unpublished drafts. The two read the same evidence and do not agree. The table is printed, and it is printed under her initials.
stops.quote: The Analytical Engine has no pretensions whatever to originate any thing. It can do whatever we know how to order it to perform. It can follow analysis; but it has no power of anticipating any analytical relations or truths.
stops.quote_source: Ada Lovelace, Note G to Menabrea's 'Sketch of the Analytical Engine', Scientific Memoirs vol. 3 (1843); archaic 'any thing' and the middle sentence restored against psychclassics.yorku.ca and en.wikiquote
sources: Allan G. Bromley, 'Difference and Analytical Engines'
Stephen Wolfram, 'Untangling the Tale of Ada Lovelace' (2015)
suggested_refs: The table of operations in Note G, Scientific Memoirs vol. 3 (1843)

stops.name: London, if harmony were susceptible of such expression
stops.date_confidence: attested to the September 1843 publication
stops.campa: In the same Note A she goes past arithmetic entirely. If the fundamental relations of pitched sounds could be put into the engine's symbols, she writes, the machine might compose music of any degree of complexity or extent. Nobody has asked a calculating machine to do this. She is describing, from inside a paper about an unbuilt brass engine, the general-purpose machine: number standing in for anything at all that can be given a rule, and the rule handed to the mechanism on cards.
stops.quote: Supposing, for instance, that the fundamental relations of pitched sounds in the science of harmony and of musical composition were susceptible of such expression and adaptations, the engine might compose elaborate and scientific pieces of music of any degree of complexity or extent.
stops.quote_source: Ada Lovelace, Note A to Menabrea's 'Sketch of the Analytical Engine', Scientific Memoirs vol. 3 (1843)
suggested_refs: Note A on the engine's non-numerical subjects

segments.name: A Calculus of the Nervous System

stops.name: Ockham Park, the tutor Carpenter
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the year is given as 1843 or 1844 in different accounts and no document is produced here
stops.campa: Annabella installs the physician and educator William Benjamin Carpenter to tutor the Lovelace children and to serve as a moral guide to their mother. Carpenter, by the account that reaches the present, attempts to turn the arrangement into an affair, and Ada ends it. Her mother's surveillance of her, begun in the schoolroom, does not stop at marriage or at a countess's title. The episode rests on biography rather than on letters that can be read, and is set down here as report.
suggested_refs: William Benjamin Carpenter's engagement in the Lovelace household

stops.name: Fyne Court, the thunder and lightning man
stops.date_confidence: the 1844 visit is attested; the day is not fixed here
stops.campa: She goes to Broomfield in the Quantocks to see Andrew Crosse, who runs insulated wire out over the trees to draw atmospheric electricity into his house and who has kept some two thousand five hundred voltaic cells at work. The country calls him the thunder and lightning man; the newspapers call him worse, since he has reported insects appearing on electrified mineral stone. She wants the apparatus and the crystallizing solutions for herself. Mathematics on paper has stopped being enough.
suggested_refs: Fyne Court, Broomfield, and Crosse's atmospheric electricity apparatus

stops.name: Ockham Park, a calculus of the nervous system
stops.date_confidence: the ambition is attested from her correspondence with Woronzow Greig; the month is conventional
stops.campa: She writes to Woronzow Greig that she means to devise a calculus of the nervous system: a mathematics of how thought and feeling move through the body, brain and nerve treated as a system with laws. She proposes it as her next work after the Notes. There is no such calculus in 1844 and no instrument that could test one. She never writes it, and she has eight years left. The proposal is the last full statement she makes of what mathematics is for, and it is a statement about bodies rather than about number.
suggested_refs: The 1844 Greig letter proposing a calculus of the nervous system

stops.name: Fyne Court, John Crosse
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the relationship is reported in the biographies without a fixed beginning, and the month is conventional
stops.campa: Through the father she meets the son. John Crosse becomes, by the biographers' account, the close and probably romantic attachment of her last eight years, and continues in some form until her death. Her husband learns some part of it at the end. The documentary basis is thinner than the certainty with which the story is usually told, and the shape of the relationship is a gap in the record rather than a settled fact. One county holds both her fairy palace and this house.
suggested_refs: The Lovelace and John Crosse connection in the 1844-1852 biographies

stops.name: Horsley Towers, the principal residence
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1845 as the year it became the principal residence
stops.campa: From 1845 Horsley Towers is the family's main house, a Tudor Revival building designed by Charles Barry in the 1820s for the banker William Currie and bought by the Kings after his death. Lovelace adds a great hall to his own designs in 1849. The Romanesque and Rhenish towers and the chapel that make the place famous come after 1859, from a European tour he takes as a widower, so she never sees them. The last years of her mathematics and her health run out inside the earlier house.
suggested_refs: The 1849 great hall at Horsley Towers, built to the Earl of Lovelace's own designs

stops.name: Epsom Downs, the syndicate
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the betting scheme and the losses are attested, but no source consulted names Epsom specifically, and the siting and the year are inferred
stops.campa: In the later 1840s she loses more than three thousand pounds on horses. She treats the racecourse as a system, and works with a syndicate of men on a mathematical method of staking meant to predict winners. The method fails. The debts run into thousands and are hidden from her husband. Five years after printing a table of operations for a machine that does not exist, she is working probability by hand against a card of races at Epsom, and the Derby takes the money.
sources: The often-repeated detail that Babbage acted as her pawnbroker for the family jewels is unsupported in the sources consulted and is not used here
suggested_refs: The 1851 staking system and the syndicate debts

stops.name: Newmarket, the card widens
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the syndicate's range beyond a single course rests on secondary accounts, with no dated letter naming Newmarket or Doncaster
stops.campa: Secondary accounts place the syndicate's wagers at Newmarket as well, England's oldest racing headquarters, the system tested across a wider card of races. The scale of the losses grows with the geography. Her letters to Babbage in these months are anxious about sums that must be found quickly and quietly. Doncaster and the St Leger appear in later retellings too, on evidence thinner still. What is documented is the debt; the itinerary is tradition built around it.
sources: Secondary biographical accounts of the gambling syndicate
Later retellings of the Doncaster wager, uncorroborated by any primary letter
suggested_refs: Newmarket and the syndicate's 1850-1851 season

stops.name: Hyde Park, the Crystal Palace
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; her personal attendance is not recorded in the Wikipedia, Britannica or Great Exhibition sources consulted, and the month is conventional
stops.campa: The Great Exhibition fills a glass building in Hyde Park with the largest assembly of industrial machinery yet gathered under one roof: looms and presses and engines, aisle after aisle of them. Babbage's calculating engines are not among the exhibits, an omission he never absorbs. She is already ill by this summer. The visit itself is not documented and stands here as the tradition it is, inside a year of which almost everything else is drawn from letters.
sources: Wikipedia, 'The Great Exhibition', which catalogues exhibits without mentioning Babbage
suggested_refs: The 1851 Great Exhibition machinery courts, Hyde Park

stops.name: Great Malvern, the water cure
stops.date_confidence: traditional; no dated stay is fixed here, and the coordinates correct a widely copied error that places Great Malvern a full degree of latitude too far south
stops.campa: As the pain worsens she goes to Great Malvern, where James Gully has run a hydropathic establishment since 1842, Holyrood House for the women and Tudor House for the men, and where Charles Darwin and Florence Nightingale are also patients. Cold baths, wet sheets, long walks on the hills. The cure does not work. Malvern takes her as one more exhausted aristocrat. Eight years earlier the patient in the wet wrapping had printed a method of computation for a machine that still does not exist.
suggested_refs: Gully's hydropathic establishment at Great Malvern, founded 1842

stops.name: London, the letter naming an executor
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Dying of cancer, she writes to Babbage asking him to act as her executor. The letter does not carry the legal authority the appointment needs, and it fails on that technicality; the story that he refused the work, unwilling to face the paperwork of her debts, is a later invention. She has known the diagnosis since at least the middle of 1851, which puts the disease a year earlier than the accounts that date it to 1852. Nineteen years after the brass engine, he is the man she asks.
sources: The Lovelace letter to Babbage, 12 August 1851
suggested_refs: The 12 August 1851 executor letter to Charles Babbage

stops.name: Harley Street, the physicians
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; no consulting room is named in the surviving letters, and the pin stands for the pattern of metropolitan consultation rather than a dated visit
stops.campa: Through 1851 and 1852 she consults a succession of London doctors. The diagnoses vary and the treatments contradict one another: rest, opium, and the bloodletting that later biographers regard as having hastened rather than eased the decline. What contemporaries call uterine cancer is understood now as most likely cervical. Her mother takes control of the sickroom, of the visitors admitted and the letters carried out, and holds that control until the end.
sources: General account of the 1851-1852 medical treatment in the biographies
suggested_refs: The Harley Street medical district in the 1850s

stops.name: Marylebone, the confession
stops.date_confidence: the date is attested; the content of the confession is an acknowledged gap and no source states what was said
stops.campa: She makes a confession to her husband. No source states what she said. William, Earl of Lovelace, withdraws from the bedside after it and does not return; the marriage ends before the life does. What she told him is one of the true blanks in her record, and every account that fills it, with John Crosse, with the debts, with something else entirely, is filling it. The hole in the paper is the fact. She has three months left, and her mother controls the room.

stops.name: Marylebone, the death
stops.date_confidence: the date and age are attested; the London address is given as Marylebone in some accounts and St James's Square in others, and the two are not reconciled here
stops.campa: She dies on 27 November 1852, thirty-six years old, the age at which her father died. The illness has taken months and the end of it is agonizing. Charles Dickens is among her acquaintances, and the story that he came at her request to read her the death of Paul Dombey circulates everywhere without a source that can be produced. She leaves three children, a mass of concealed debt, a set of notes on an unbuilt machine, and a name that will take a century to be read on its own terms.
sources: The Dickens deathbed reading is not in the Wikipedia article, which lists him only among her acquaintances; treated as unsourced

stops.name: Hucknall, beside Byron
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: At her own request she is buried in the Byron vault at the Church of St Mary Magdalene in Hucknall, beside the father who saw her once, at five weeks old. The vault has held the poet since 1824. The parish register enters her as Augusta Ada, Countess of Lovelace, above the vault that holds the poet. Her mother, who spent thirty-six years training the poet out of her, does not get the last word on where she lies. Visitors come to the church for two names now, and not always in that order.

stops.name: Washington, the language called Ada
stops.date_confidence: attested; the pin is the canonical Washington point already used in this atlas for Hollerith's census machine
stops.campa: The United States Department of Defense approves the reference manual for a new programming language and calls it Ada. The military standard number is 1815, her birth year, and the approval date is 10 December, her birthday. The card lineage she described in 1843 has by then run through Herman Hollerith's census tabulator on this same ground in 1890, through Tony Skyrme's implosion calculations at Los Alamos, John von Neumann's machines and Claude Shannon's chess programme, and out the other side into electricity.
sources: ANSI/MIL-STD-1815A Ada Reference Manual, U.S. Department of Defense

stops.name: London, the first edition sold
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: The one privately held copy of the 1843 Scientific Memoirs printing containing her Notes is sold at auction in London for ninety-five thousand pounds to an anonymous buyer. Five other copies are known, all institutional. In the same decade a New York newspaper runs the obituary it never printed in 1852, and the British passport puts her face beside Babbage's. Her married surname sits in the Bodleian too, on the Lovelace Collection of John Locke's manuscripts, named for the earls she married into.

stops.name: Millbank, the bronze
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: A bronze of her by Etienne and Mary Millner, worked from Margaret Sarah Carpenter's 1836 portrait, is unveiled at Millbank on International Women's Day. In the same year Nvidia names a graphics processor architecture Ada Lovelace. A Grade II listed memorial already stands at Kirkby Mallory, in the village her mother carried her to at five weeks old. The name goes to machinery now: a programming language in 1980, a processor architecture in 2022, and in both cases the machine is the general-purpose kind.

stops.name: National Portrait Gallery, the three photographs
stops.date_confidence: the acquisition is dated to 2025; the day is not fixed here and the daguerreotypes are dated only to about 1843
stops.campa: The National Portrait Gallery acquires the only three known photographs of her: two daguerreotypes taken by Antoine Claudet around 1843, and one photograph of Henry Wyndham Phillips's portrait. The daguerreotypes are contemporary with the Notes, which puts the face and the algorithm in the same months. She spent her life being looked at as Byron's daughter. The images enter a national collection under her own name, one hundred and seventy-three years after her death.
